Senses.Explanation: The first graph means “small or minor” (小); the second means “assemble for instruction” (參) (as in 上堂 the great convocation and 晚參 the evening gathering). (小參) is the informal, lesser convocation, set against (上堂) (ascending the hall — the great, formal convocation). The monastic code (敕修百丈清規) defines it plainly: "the small convocation has no fixed place" (小參初無定所), held wherever suits the size of the assembly — the sleeping hall (寢堂) or the teaching hall (法堂) — announced by hanging a (小參牌) and given at the evening bell (昏鐘); hence its stock form "that evening's small convocation" (當晚小參) and (晚小參). The rule adds that the abbot "just as at the five-day (上堂)," (登座) so (小參) is procedurally the same address, only informal in place and timing. In the yulu it is a genre heading paralleling (上堂) in the table of contents (卷第八　上堂八　小參一). The code's fuller definition names occasions and register: (如住持入院)。(或官員檀越入山)。(或受人特請)。(或謂亡者開示)。(或四節臘則移於昏鐘鳴)。(而謂之小參)。(可以敘世禮)。(曰家教者是也)。(然亦不鳴放參鐘)。(謂猶有參也) (when the abbot takes office, or officials and donors come up the mountain, or on a special request, or as instruction for the dead, or at the four season-nodes — moved to the sounding of the evening bell it is called 小參; worldly courtesies may be recounted; this is what is meant by the 'house teaching' 家教; yet the release-bell is still not rung, meaning there is still convocation; T48n2025 1119c07), and its procedure: (至日午後)。(侍者覆住持云令客頭行者報眾)。(掛小參牌)。(當晚不鳴放參鐘)。(昏鐘鳴時行者覆住持)。(鳴鼓一通)。(眾集兩序歸位)。(住持登座提綱) (T48n2025 1119c12). A yulu preserves a live exchange about the word itself, set against (大參): (我曾問副寺師)：『(如何是小參)？』(寺曰)：『(吃粥)。』『(如何是大參)？』(寺曰)：『(吃飯)。』 (what is the small convocation? — eating gruel; and the great convocation? — eating rice; J37nB390, which also narrates 已掛小參牌了也). Occasion-prefixed forms carry most of its deployment: (當晚小參) 127 hits/62 texts, (晚小參) 160/81, (除夜)·(歲夜小參) 95/45, (解制)·(結制小參) 29/21.
Senses.Note: A genre / format marker, not a thesis. Distinguished from (上堂) by informality: no fixed place, evening timing, smaller occasion; very often (當晚小參) / (晚小參). The abbot's procedure otherwise matches (上堂). Cf. (晚參). Zen-scoped grep (tag-stripped, 2026-07-11): (小參) 7023 hits in 337 allowlist texts (上堂: 54942 in 402) — both pervasive genre headings; (小參牌) 3 hits in 2 texts (T48n2025, J37nB390).

AlternateTargets: what is the purport of that?
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'what is the intent or purport?' It is a stock second-round question in recorded exchanges. A monk first asks, 'What is buddha?' The teacher answers, 'Spread the hair to cover the mud; lay the body crosswise on the ground.' The monk then asks, 'What is the purport?' and the teacher replies, 'Even Papiyan would furrow his brow.' The intensified form, 'I have not yet examined it—what is the purport?', likewise follows an answer: after a monk asks the intent of the ancestral teacher's coming from the west, the teacher gives a line about an old temple being difficult to read; the monk presses with the intensified question. The formula also follows a raised earlier saying. A monk quotes 'play a ball on swift water,' asks its purport, and receives 'thought after thought does not stop or remain.' In another exchange the first answer is 'the eyebrows divide into the figure eight'; the press receives 'both ears hang to the shoulders.' The phrase asks about the immediately preceding saying and does not supply that saying's answer itself.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide conversational formula, not a master's coinage. Current count: 3,178 matches in 292 files; the intensified 'I have not yet examined it—what is the purport?' has 194 matches in 45 files, and 'what is the teacher's purport?' has 13 in 12. It occurs after a first-round answer and after quotations of earlier cases. All selected witnesses are two-speaker or raised-case passages, so their occurrence master keys remain null.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, dim or dull (昏) sinking (沈). Dahui supplies the corpus's clearest direct description: forgetting or blanking out falls into the ghost cave beneath Black Mountain, and the teachings call this dull sinking; he contrasts it with deliberate attention, whose thought-consciousness flies about and is called agitation. Other records label dull sinking “not good” beside “binding thought strays from the real” and pair it repeatedly with agitation as the two named conditions found in the Chan hall. The Chan record also bends the inherited fault-category against simple rejection: Gaofeng says the four graphs “dull sinking and agitation” are themselves buddha-nature, Daodu calls the pair one's place for establishing life, and Dahui tells Lü Juren that whether dull-sunk or agitated, it is still only Lü Juren. The deviation lies in this combination of exact diagnosis, fixed pairing, and masters' refusal to locate the named condition outside the person who reports it.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 51 exact occurrences in 29 allowlisted files. The dominant fixed pair is “dull sinking and agitation” (昏沈掉舉), with sinking or forgetting contrasted against agitation or deliberate attention. Written variants are “dull sinking” (昏沈), “dull sinking” with the water-radical form (昏沉), and “dull sinking” with the alternate first graph (昬沈).

Senses.Explanation: To leak out or show through. Chan records most often use the expression as a retrospective appraisal after someone has spoken or acted: 'it leaked out,' 'quite a lot leaked out,' 'the whole body leaked out,' or 'one could not avoid leaking once.' Foyan applies the same verdict in succession to Deshan's statement that his house has no phrases and no single thing to give people, Xuefeng's statement that he went empty-handed and returned empty-handed, and Muzhou's calling a monk a board-carrying fellow. The Blue Cliff Record says that much had leaked out when Bodhidharma pressed Emperor Wu at the outset. A later direct question, 'What is the place of leaking out?' receives a list of recorded expressions and objects: Yunmen's flatbread, Zhaozhou's tea, Xuefeng's wooden ball, and Zihu's dog. The records do not identify a single substance that leaks, and this entry adds none.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 488 matches in 172 files. 'It leaked out' occurs sixty times in thirty-seven files; 'quite a lot leaked out' occurs eighty-one times in fifty-four; 'the whole body leaked out' occurs twice in two; and 'could not avoid leaking out' occurs twice in two. One passage in one file directly asks where leaking out is. The two nominal-looking matches ending in 'one who leaks' are parts of late verse lines about a portrait or a festival wrapper and do not supply a separate definition.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a golden-scaled fish through the net
AlternateTargets: the golden fish that has passed through the net
Senses.Explanation: Literally “a golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net,” attested 257 times in 120 allowlisted texts. The phrase is anchored in Sansheng’s public question to Xuefeng: “What does the golden-scaled fish through the net feed on?” (透網金鱗未審以何為食); Xuefeng replies that he will tell him after he comes out of the net. Yuanwu’s prose supplies the corpus’s direct definition: “only with an eye at the crown is one called a golden-scaled fish through the net” (頂門有眼方謂之透網金鱗). The image then becomes an appraisal of monks: one teacher hails a monk as “excellent—a patch-robed monk, a golden-scaled fish through the net” (俊哉衲子，透網金鱗), while later interviews ask why such a fish is still held up by water.
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is the fish-and-net image functioning as a public question and a teacher’s appraisal of a monk, with the Blue Cliff Record's explicit crown-eye formula. The fish, the case question, and later appraisals refer to the same corpus image; they are deployment shapes rather than separate senses. In the family check, “golden-scaled fish” (金鱗) is broader, while “through the net” (透網) supplies the defining escaped-net morphology.

Senses.Explanation: A verb-object phrase: "pass completely through" (透) the "barrier" or "pass" (關), attested 266 times in 112 allowlisted texts. A Huanglong retrospective distinguishes the one who has passed from one who has not: "one who has already passed the barrier swings his arms and goes straight on—how would he know there is a gatekeeper? One who asks the gatekeeper whether he may pass is one who has not passed the barrier" (已過關者掉臂徑去，安知有關吏；從吏問可否，此未透關者也). Zhongfeng Mingben records a corrective contrast: people thread all the old and new public cases onto one string and call this "passing the barrier," while "the tight barrier of life and death beneath their heels has not actually been passed" (盡將古今公案一串穿却謂之透關；脚跟下一座生死牢關，政好不曾透得). The phrase also builds the recurrent noun "an eye that passes the barrier" (透關眼, 97 occurrences), used by Yuanwu and later speakers to ask whether anyone present has such an eye, and the rare "phrase that passes the barrier" (透關句, 1). Chijue Daochong's exchange says, "passing the barrier must be [done with] an eye that passes the barrier; returning a treasure takes one who can distinguish treasures" (透關須是透關眼，得寶還佗別寶人). These are recorded descriptions, corrections, and compounds; this entry adds no unrecorded destination beyond the barrier.
Senses.Note: The attributive forms "one who has passed the barrier" (已透關者) and "one who has not passed the barrier" (未透關者) occur 12 and 14 times respectively. The broader verbs "get through" (透得) and "pass through" (透過) occur 1,057 and 624 times and are not counted as headword occurrences unless followed by the graph for barrier. Zhongfeng explicitly distinguishes passing through language from passing the tight barrier underfoot; that text-drawn distinction is retained.
